title: HTTP Cookies & Web Auth: The Field Manual
summary: A dense working guide to HTTP cookies — every attribute, how scoping and SameSite actually behave, and how cookies underpin session vs token authentication. Covers mechanics, security flags, trade-offs, and the mistakes that break logins or leak accounts.

chapters.title: Why Cookies Exist: State on a Stateless Protocol
points: HTTP is stateless: every request is independent, server remembers nothing between them
Cookie = small key-value string the server asks the browser to store and replay on later requests
Server sets with response header `Set-Cookie: sid=abc123`; browser replays with `Cookie: sid=abc123`
One `Set-Cookie` header per cookie — you cannot comma-join multiple cookies in one header
Browser sends ALL matching cookies in a single `Cookie` header, `; ` separated: `Cookie: sid=abc; theme=dark`
Cookies are sent automatically by the browser — no JavaScript needed, and that automatic-ness is the root of CSRF
Original spec: Netscape 1994; current spec RFC 6265bis (SameSite, prefixes, size limits)
Size limit: ~4096 bytes per cookie (name+value+attributes); browsers cap ~50 cookies per domain, ~180 total
Cookies cost bandwidth: they ride on EVERY matching request, including images and CSS — 4KB cookie × 50 assets = 200KB wasted
Three storage rivals: cookie (auto-sent, server-readable), localStorage (JS-only, never auto-sent), sessionStorage (JS-only, per-tab)
Rule of thumb: cookie for anything the server needs; localStorage for client-only UI state
Cookie value must be URL-encoded — raw `;`, `,`, space, and `=` in a value break parsing
Cookies are not encrypted by default — the browser stores them in plaintext on disk (or an OS keystore); sign or encrypt anything you trust
Common uses: session ID, auth token, CSRF token, locale, A/B test bucket, analytics ID, consent record

chapters.title: Anatomy of Set-Cookie: Every Attribute
points: Full form: `Set-Cookie: name=value; Domain=x; Path=/; Expires=...; Max-Age=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Partitioned`
`name=value` is the only required part; everything after `;` is an attribute
`Domain` — which hosts receive the cookie; omitted means host-only (exact host, no subdomains)
`Path` — URL path prefix that must match; defaults to the directory of the setting request, not `/`
`Expires=<HTTP-date>` — absolute expiry in GMT: `Expires=Wed, 09 Jun 2027 10:18:14 GMT`
`Max-Age=<seconds>` — relative lifetime; `Max-Age=0` or negative deletes the cookie immediately
`Max-Age` beats `Expires` when both are present (all modern browsers)
No `Expires` and no `Max-Age` = session cookie: dies when the browser closes (but 'restore tabs' can resurrect it)
`Secure` — only sent over HTTPS; `HttpOnly` — hidden from `document.cookie`; `SameSite` — cross-site send policy
`Partitioned` (CHIPS) — third-party cookie keyed by the top-level site, one jar per embedding site
Attributes are NOT sent back: the `Cookie` header carries only `name=value` pairs — the server cannot read a cookie's own Path or Expires
Unknown attributes are silently ignored — a typo like `HttpOnley` fails with zero errors, which is why flags go unset in production
Attribute names are case-insensitive (`secure` == `Secure`); cookie NAMES are case-sensitive (`sid` != `SID`)
Deleting a cookie means re-setting it with the same name, Domain, and Path plus `Max-Age=0` — mismatched Domain/Path leaves a zombie copy
Server-side helper example (Express): `res.cookie('sid', id, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: 86400000 })`

chapters.title: Scoping I: Domain and the Subdomain Trap
points: No `Domain` attribute = host-only cookie: set on `app.example.com`, sent ONLY to `app.example.com`
`Domain=example.com` = sent to `example.com` AND every subdomain (`api.`, `www.`, `blog.`, `evil-tenant.`)
Leading dot is legacy: `Domain=.example.com` is normalized to `Domain=example.com` — identical behavior today
You cannot widen upward: `app.example.com` cannot set `Domain=com` or `Domain=other.com` — browser rejects the cookie silently
You cannot set a cookie for a sibling: `a.example.com` cannot target `b.example.com`, only the shared parent
Public Suffix List (PSL) blocks setting cookies on registrable suffixes like `.com`, `.co.uk`, `github.io` — the 'supercookie' defense
Default host-only is the safer default; add `Domain` only when subdomains genuinely need the cookie
Subdomain trap: an XSS or takeover on `blog.example.com` can read AND overwrite a `Domain=example.com` session cookie
Cookie tossing attack: a compromised subdomain sets a cookie with the same name on the parent domain to shadow or fixate the real one
Port is NOT part of cookie scope: `example.com:3000` and `example.com:8080` share one cookie jar — a dev-server footgun
Scheme is only partly part of scope: `Secure` cookies are HTTPS-only, but a non-Secure cookie set over HTTP is readable over HTTPS and vice versa
Cookies ignore the same-origin policy — they use 'site' (registrable domain), which is looser than origin
Origin = scheme + host + port; site = eTLD+1. `https://a.example.com` and `http://b.example.com:8080` are different origins, same site
Practical pattern: give each tenant/app its own host-only cookie; only SSO cookies deserve a parent `Domain`

chapters.title: Scoping II: Path, Prefixes, and Precedence
points: `Path=/admin` sends the cookie to `/admin`, `/admin/`, and `/admin/users` — but NOT `/administrator`
Match rule: the cookie path must be a prefix ending at a `/` boundary or exactly equal to the request path
Default path is derived from the setting URL's directory: a response from `/app/login` defaults to `Path=/app` — a classic 'cookie vanished' bug
Always set `Path=/` for session cookies unless you have a hard reason not to
Path is NOT a security boundary: same-origin JavaScript can read cookies at any path via iframe tricks; use it for organization only
Multiple cookies can share a name at different paths — the browser sends all of them, `Cookie: sid=a; sid=b`
Send order: longer Path first; equal paths break ties by creation time (oldest first) — servers usually read just the first, so shadowing is easy
The server cannot tell which sent cookie came from which Path — a real source of 'logged in as the wrong user' bugs
`__Secure-` prefix: browser rejects the cookie unless it has `Secure` and was set over HTTPS
`__Host-` prefix: requires `Secure`, `Path=/`, and NO `Domain` attribute — locks the cookie to the exact host
`__Host-` is the strongest anti-cookie-tossing defense: no subdomain can overwrite it. Use `__Host-session` for auth
Example: `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=abc; Secure; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`
Prefixes are enforced by the browser, not the server — the name is the contract
Overwriting rule: a cookie is 'the same cookie' only if name + Domain + Path all match; otherwise you get a duplicate, not an update

chapters.title: Secure and HttpOnly: The Two Cheapest Wins
points: `Secure` = browser only sends the cookie over HTTPS (localhost is exempted for development)
Without `Secure`, one plain-HTTP request on hostile Wi-Fi leaks the session ID in cleartext — sslstrip in one line
`Secure` restricts SENDING, not writing: pre-RFC6265bis, plain HTTP could still overwrite a Secure cookie; modern browsers now block that
`HttpOnly` = `document.cookie` cannot read or write it — the value is invisible to page JavaScript
`HttpOnly` does not stop XSS; it stops token EXFILTRATION. An attacker with XSS can still ride the session by firing same-origin fetches
That is why `HttpOnly` pairs with CSRF defense and short sessions — it raises cost, not a wall
`HttpOnly` cookies are still visible in DevTools' Application tab and in the network trace — it is not obfuscation
Rule: every auth cookie gets `Secure` + `HttpOnly` + `SameSite` + `__Host-` prefix. Non-negotiable
A CSRF token cookie is the standard exception — the double-submit pattern needs JS to read it, so it is deliberately non-HttpOnly
HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) complements `Secure` by removing the first plaintext request entirely
Ordering gotcha: setting a cookie without `Secure` on an HTTP redirect page, then upgrading, leaves a leaked copy
Checklist for prod: no auth cookie without `Secure`; no auth cookie readable from JS; both verified in the browser, not the code
Testing: `curl -i https://site/login | grep -i set-cookie` shows exactly what the browser will store
Local dev workaround: use `https://localhost` with a self-signed cert rather than dropping `Secure` conditionally — conditionals ship to prod

chapters.title: SameSite: Lax, Strict, None
points: SameSite controls whether a cookie rides on CROSS-SITE requests — the browser-level CSRF mitigation
'Site' means eTLD+1 (registrable domain), so `a.example.com` → `b.example.com` is same-site, not cross-site
`SameSite=Strict` — never sent on any cross-site request, including a plain link click from another site
Strict's cost: click a link from email or Google to your logged-in app and the first page renders logged OUT
`SameSite=Lax` — sent on top-level GET navigations (link clicks, `window.location`), blocked on POST, iframe, `fetch`, `img`, and `XHR`
`SameSite=None` — always sent, but the browser REQUIRES `Secure` or the cookie is rejected entirely
Default when the attribute is omitted: modern Chrome/Firefox/Edge treat it as `Lax`; older browsers treated it as `None`
'Lax + POST' subtlety: Chrome once gave newly set cookies a 2-minute grace window where cross-site POST still worked — never rely on it
Safari/ITP historically blocked all third-party cookies regardless of SameSite — test on Safari separately
Choose Strict for banking-grade actions and admin panels; Lax as the default for normal app sessions
Choose None+Secure only for genuine third-party embeds: SSO iframes, payment widgets, embedded chat
Lax still allows cross-site GET, so a GET that mutates state (`/delete?id=5`) is CSRF-able even with Lax — never mutate on GET
Two-cookie pattern: a Lax 'read' session for smooth link entry plus a Strict cookie required for state-changing routes
SameSite is defense in depth, not a CSRF replacement — keep tokens for older browsers and for same-site XSS
CHIPS / `Partitioned`: for third-party contexts, one cookie jar per top-level site so the cookie cannot track across sites

chapters.title: Session Auth: Server-Side State
points: Flow: POST credentials → server verifies → creates a session record → returns an opaque session ID in a cookie
The cookie holds ONLY a random ID; all real data (user ID, roles, expiry) lives server-side in Redis, Postgres, or memory
Session ID must be cryptographically random and ≥128 bits: `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` — never a counter or UUIDv1
Every request: browser sends cookie → server looks up the session store → attaches the user → handles the request
Logout is instant and real: delete the server-side record and the ID becomes worthless everywhere
Revocation is the headline advantage — ban a user, force-logout every device, invalidate on password change
Cost: a store lookup per request, plus a shared store once you run more than one server process
Sticky sessions and in-memory stores break horizontal scaling — the classic 'random logouts after deploy' bug
Session fixation: ALWAYS regenerate the session ID on login and on privilege change (`req.session.regenerate()`)
Absolute timeout (max lifetime, e.g. 12h) plus idle timeout (e.g. 30 min of inactivity) — implement both
Rolling sessions extend the expiry on each request; nice UX, but pair with an absolute cap or sessions live forever
Store the session's IP and user-agent to detect obvious hijacking, but do not hard-bind — mobile IPs change constantly
Signed cookie sessions (Rails/Flask style) put the data IN the cookie with an HMAC — no store, but no revocation, and the 4KB cap bites
Session store TTL must be set at the store level (Redis `EXPIRE`) or dead sessions accumulate forever

chapters.title: Token Auth: JWT and the Bearer Model
points: A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots: `header.payload.signature` — self-contained, no server lookup
Header names the algorithm (`{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`); payload holds claims; signature covers header+payload
Standard claims: `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti` — `exp` and `aud` are the ones people forget to verify
Base64 is ENCODING, not encryption: anyone can read a JWT payload. Never put a password, PII, or a secret in it
HS256 = one shared secret (simple, but every verifier can also mint). RS256/ES256 = private key signs, public key verifies — right for multi-service
The `alg: none` attack and the HS256/RS256 confusion attack both come from trusting the header — pin the expected algorithm server-side
Core trade-off: stateless verification is fast and scales flat, but you cannot revoke a token before `exp`
Revocation workarounds: very short access tokens (5–15 min), a denylist by `jti`, or a token version column checked per request — each reintroduces state
Refresh token pattern: short-lived access token in memory or a cookie + long-lived refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie on a narrow `Path=/auth/refresh`
Refresh token rotation: each refresh issues a new one and invalidates the old; a reused old token means theft — kill the whole family
'Store JWT in localStorage' is the popular bad advice: any XSS reads it instantly, with no `HttpOnly` protection available
Better: put the JWT in a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite` cookie — you get the XSS protection back and take on CSRF, which is easier to defend
Bearer tokens in an `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` header are immune to CSRF because the browser never adds them automatically
JWTs are genuinely right for: cross-service auth, mobile and native clients, third-party APIs, and short-lived one-off grants
Clock skew: allow a small leeway (30–60s) on `exp`/`nbf` or distributed servers reject valid tokens

chapters.title: Session vs Token: The Comparison Table
points: State: session = server-side store; token = self-contained, nothing stored
Revocation: session = instant delete; token = impossible until `exp` without adding a denylist
Scaling: session = shared store is a dependency and a bottleneck; token = stateless, no lookup, scales flat
Per-request cost: session = one store round trip (~1ms Redis); token = one signature verification (~0.1ms CPU)
Payload size: session cookie ~32–64 bytes; JWT ~200–800 bytes on every single request
Cross-domain: session cookies are constrained by cookie scoping; tokens travel anywhere in a header
Mobile/native clients: cookies are awkward outside a browser jar; tokens are the natural fit
XSS exposure: HttpOnly session cookie is unreadable; localStorage token is fully exposed
CSRF exposure: cookie-based auth needs SameSite plus tokens; header-based bearer auth is immune by construction
Complexity: sessions are simpler to get right; token auth needs refresh, rotation, and key management
Default recommendation: server-rendered app or first-party SPA on one domain → sessions in `__Host-` cookies
Use tokens when: multiple backend services, a public API, native mobile apps, or third-party integrations
Hybrid, and very common: session cookie for the browser UI, short-lived JWT minted for service-to-service calls
Neither choice fixes bad auth: rate-limit login, hash with argon2/bcrypt, and MFA matter more than the transport

chapters.title: Mistakes, Debugging, and the Checklist
points: Missing `Secure`/`HttpOnly` in production because the dev config was copied — assert flags in a startup check, not a code review
Default `Path` swallowing the cookie: cookie set at `/api/login` never reaches `/dashboard`. Always `Path=/`
Delete fails because Domain/Path do not match the original — the cookie survives and the user stays logged in
Two cookies with the same name (one host-only, one `Domain=`) — the server reads the wrong one; inspect the raw `Cookie` header, not the parsed map
`SameSite=None` without `Secure` = the browser drops the cookie entirely, with only a console warning
OAuth callbacks and payment redirects break under `SameSite=Strict` because the return is a cross-site POST
No session regeneration on login = session fixation: attacker plants an ID, victim logs in, attacker owns the session
Storing a JWT in localStorage 'for convenience' — one XSS and every token leaves the building
Trusting a cookie value as input: cookies are fully attacker-controlled. Sign, validate, and never SQL-interpolate them
4KB overflow silently truncates or drops the cookie — happens when roles or flash messages get stuffed into a signed cookie session
Cookies not sent on `fetch` cross-origin: you need `credentials: 'include'` client-side AND `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` with an explicit origin (never `*`) server-side
Debug tools: DevTools → Application → Cookies (shows every flag), `curl -v`, `document.cookie` (HttpOnly cookies are invisible there — that is the point)
Chrome logs cookie rejections in the Network tab's Cookies pane with a reason — check it before blaming the server
Ship checklist: `__Host-` prefix, `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`, absolute + idle timeout, regenerate on login, delete server-side on logout
One-line summary: cookies are automatic, scoped by site not origin, and attacker-visible — so sign them, flag them, scope them tight, and keep the real state on the server
